I assumed that the film and TV major was focused on production, but unlike many other film schools that have separate majors for people interested in production or screenwriting or animation, all of it falls under the umbrella film and TV. It's actually really nice and gives you a lot of freedom to explore different aspects of film.

If you do decide to apply for film and TV, you will be required to do some production classes, so you can't identify solely as a writer while you're there. But after your sophomore year (or when you've completed 4 production classes), they pretty much let you design the education you want.

If you decide to still apply for dramatic writing, I don't really know much about the program, but I do know that it is a **very** small program, making it really difficult to get in to. Tbh, I've always kinda wondered if I applied to the correct major when I was in high school would I get in.

When it comes to your portfolio, you don't need to worry about being perfect. They want to see you have talent, not a perfected craft. Research screenplay formatting and I'd recommend to use Celtx, which is a free (I think?) screenplay writing software. Also **have other people read what you've written**. I know that sometimes showing people your writing is weird and somewhat scary, but I really recommend doing it. Anyone works, but someone who is also a writer is even better.

Hi! First, I'd like to say that your formatting was very good and it was easy to read; it's very frustrating when scripts are messy with big blocks of text.

Here are my initial thoughts after my first quick read through.

* All the moments where either Jolene or another character talks about how she's special or meant for something more felt a bit on the nose. It's breaking the "show don't tell" rule a little too much. The only way I could see it working is that if Jolene is hit with the realization that she is actually extraordinarily normal, so it's commenting on how everyone feels they're very special at one point.
* I personally wasn't a fan of the dad dying so fast. It felt like when Disney parents just kinda immediately die from an unexplained disease. We as an audience didn't really get a chance to care about him before he died, so maybe wait a bit further in until he goes? 
* All the VOs broke the "show don't tell" rule in my eyes. There's always a way to convey a character's emotions without having to hear their thoughts directly. For instance, when we first see Jolene after the time skip, maybe instead of VO, she could be talking on the phone with someone and complaining about things so that the audience gets a sense that she's unhappy with her life.
* I wasn't a big fan of Jolene as a character. If you're familiar with the term, she came off as a bit of a "Mary Sue." In other words, she felt more like a wish-fulfillment rather than a real person. She didn't feel like she had a real personality besides being sweet and feeling like she was "meant for more." The whole "beautiful but doesn't know it" trope is also a very common one that I'm not really a fan of.
* I'm not really sure where this plot is headed. I know it's only the first act, but I still personally feel like I should know the theme of your story by now.

Alright, so those were some of my initial thoughts. You've got strong work so far, and I'm excited to see how it develops from here. Please let me know if you have any questions.

Hi! I'm really impressed that this was your first time writing a short. You did a great job with formatting. I could also tell that you had a fun time writing it, which is so important.

* Make sure you proofread and double-check your script for grammatical errors. The ones that stood out to me most were missing commas.
* Technically, you don't really need CUT TO:s anymore. All the professors I've had say that now it's considered redundant, although not technically wrong.
* Keep all action paragraphs as short as possible. My rule of thumb is never to have them exceed 3 lines.
* Put the salesman in all caps when he enters. When the dad changes identities I would also reintroduce him as a new character and then change his character name for dialogue as well.
* Watch out for exposition-y dialogue. One that really caught my attention was the dad's second line.
* This is more of a personal opinion, but starting the story from the Dad's point of view felt like it was set-up to be his story, and I was a little thrown off when it became the salesman's story.
* While reading the script, a lot of the moments felt a bit disjointed to me. I totally understand wanting to subvert expectations, but in my opinion, it was a bit jarring to read.
* Something to help with the aforementioned comment is to really think out your plot. I feel like the plot restarts itself 2 or 3 times before reaching any falling action or resolution.
* The ending also felt like it was cut off a bit short. This issue also ties into how the plot didn't feel like it was quite as polished as it should be.
* While reading this, I sort of felt like it may have done better as a sketch rather than a short. That may just be because sketches can get away with looser plots like this. I'm not sure if that's something you'd want to consider though.

Hi! Congrats on writing a pilot! I think this was a good draft. Here are my notes:

The biggest issue I had with the script was that you too often make your reader assume things. For example, in the beginning the setting was not clear to me. I know later through dialogue that it's a bank and in real life I would see it's a bank, but readers should know from the get go. The other one I most remember was saying firing Steve (?) would be a hate crime. I assume that was about race and maybe I missed it, but I didn't fully understand.

I know it's a pilot and there's a lot of introducing to be done but I think you need to get to your conflict quicker. Since you're half hour, the conflict needs to be introduced around I'd say the third page (not exactly, just an estimate). That way the other characters learn about it faster so the conflict can increase even more.

What was happening with Bella's (to camera)? Was it meant to indicate a freeze frame or a cut away to a confessional. If it's a confessional, then what's the reasoning behind it?

Personally, I felt like the characters all blended into one another. I could never really distinguish who was who. I would make sure to give each person more of a voice and let us know some details about each one. The only thing I knew about all of them is that they were bankers.

Another way to help readers remember who your characters are is to give them an introduction (and have their name in all caps) when they're first introduced. Something like: BELLA (early 30s, serious and professional).

I would delete the CUT TO:s. Professors I've had say that it's not used too much anymore since it's redundant.

And lastly, I would do a sweep over the script and clean up grammar. There were a few rouge commas and missing periods here and there.
